FARRA:v3p203/r10.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p203/r10.speaker: كثير من الناس
FARRA:v3p203/r10.claim: Many readers instead use idh adbara, with hamza and idh.

FARRA:v3p203/r8.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p203/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
FARRA:v3p203/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads wa-l-layli idhā dabara, with idhā and the verb without hamza.

FARRA:v3p203/r9.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p203/r9.speaker: مجاهد وبعض أهل المدينة
FARRA:v3p203/r9.claim: Mujāhid and some Medinan readers likewise use idhā dabara.

FARRA:v3p204/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p204/r1.speaker: عبد الله
FARRA:v3p204/r1.claim: ʿAbd Allāh's reading has idhā adbara, with hamza.

FARRA:v3p204/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p204/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
FARRA:v3p204/r3.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās gives the reading idhā dabara.

FARRA:v3p204/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p204/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
FARRA:v3p204/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains adbara by analogy with the back of a camel, using the verb for turning its back.

FARRA:v3p204/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p204/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
FARRA:v3p204/r5.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd reads adbara; al-Farrāʾ says the report lacks idh and treats dabara and adbara as dialect variants.

FARRA:v3p204/r6.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p204/r6.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p204/r6.claim: Dabara and adbara are equivalent for night, day, winter, and summer; for a rider, however, Arabs use the form with hamza.

TAB-FULL:v23p442/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r1.claim: The oath refutes the claim that Hell's keepers would be enough to drive the Prophet's companions away; God swears by the moon and departing night.

TAB-FULL:v23p442/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r2.claim: The night is described as departing and going away.

TAB-FULL:v23p442/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r3.claim: Qatāda glosses the night as having departed.

TAB-FULL:v23p442/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās instead describes the night as darkening.

TAB-FULL:v23p442/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r5.claim: Most Medinan and Basran readers read idh adbara, while some Meccan and Kufan readers read idhā dabara; al-Ṭabarī accepts both as valid and equivalent dialect forms.

TAB-FULL:v23p442/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r6.speaker: بعض الكوفيين
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r6.claim: Some Kufans call the forms dialectal pairs: dabbara/adbara and qabila/aqbala, while using the prefixed form for a rider's coming or going.

TAB-FULL:v23p442/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r7.speaker: بعض البصريين
TAB-FULL:v23p442/r7.claim: Some Basrans say dabara means the day has passed and is at its end, while adbara means turned away; Al-Ṭabarī prefers that both readings mean the same and cites Arabic usage and interpreters' lack of distinction.

ZAJJAJ:v5p248#2/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p248#2/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p248#2/r2.claim: Both adbara and dubira are sound Arabic for night’s departure; similarly, night may be said to approach or come.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3384/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3384/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3384/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the night departing as its darkness.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3384/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3384/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3384/r2.claim: Mujahid says Ibn Abbas demonstrated the night departing by calling to him at the first call to prayer near dawn.

NAHHAS:v5p70/r10.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p70/r10.speaker: أبو عبيد
NAHHAS:v5p70/r10.claim: Abū ʿUbayd prefers idhā because the next oath uses idhā; Abu Jaʿfar replies that God may swear by what He wills, with no requirement that both forms match in time.

NAHHAS:v5p70/r9.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p70/r9.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p70/r9.claim: The named readers divide between idh adbara and idhā adbara; Abu Jaʿfar says both verbs mean the same according to exegetes and most linguists.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r1.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وأبو بكر عن عاصم وابن عامر والكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r1.claim: These readers say دَبَرَ with fatḥa on dāl, the form Yunus glosses as having passed or ended.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r2.speaker: نافع وعاصم في رواية حفص وحمزة
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r2.claim: These readers say أَدْبَرَ with a still dāl; Yunus distinguishes it as having turned away.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r3.speaker: يونس
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r3.claim: Yunus distinguishes دبر, 'ended,' from أدبر, 'turned away,' while also explaining the phrases about the stars and prostrations as their decline or aftermath.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r4.speaker: الحسن
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r4.claim: Al-Ḥasan interprets the setting of the stars as the two dawn rakʿahs and the aftermath of prostration as two rakʿahs after sunset; reports from Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās illustrate the phrase as night turns away.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r5.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r5.speaker: قتادة
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p338#2/r5.claim: Qatādah explains the night as having departed, and the poet's expression 'yesterday that had passed' supports both forms.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r10.speaker: أبو عبيدة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r10.claim: It may mean when the night arrives as the day withdraws.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r11.speaker: الحسن وأبو عبد الرحمن وابن مسعود وأبي بن كعب
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r11.claim: They read دبر instead of أدبر.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r12.speaker: الأخفش
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r12.claim: Akhfash says أدبر and دبر are two forms with the same meaning.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r13.speaker: أبو عبيدة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r13.claim: Abu Ubayda distinguishes them: دبر is when something is behind you, while أدبر is when it turns away ahead of you.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r14.speaker: ابن بحر
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r14.claim: Ibn Bahr distinguishes دبر as following what came before and أدبر as departing.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r9.claim: The night when it withdraws means when it has departed.

QUSHAYRI:v3p364/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p364/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p364/r9.claim: A reading without the alif, dabbara, means that the night has passed.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:74:32-39/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:74:32-39/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:74:32-39/r2.claim: The night “when it recedes” means it comes after the day.

JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r1.speaker: نافع وحفص عن عاصم ويعقوب
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r1.claim: They read wa-l-layli idh with idh and no alif in the next word; the remaining readers use idhā. Both dabbara and adbara are valid forms.

JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r2.speaker: أبو حاتم
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r2.claim: Abu Hatim argues for idhā because Qur'anic oaths use idhā, not idh.

JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r3.speaker: أبو عبيد
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r3.claim: Abu Ubayd prefers idhā because it parallels the following oath, waṣ-ṣubḥi idhā asfar.

JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r4.claim: Both recitations of idh and idhā are sound and evident; neither has priority over the other.

JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r5.speaker: أبو مسلم
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r5.claim: Abu Muslim explains dabbara as coming immediately after daytime, the opposite of adbara, which means turning away and departing.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p271#2/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p271#2/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p271#2/r8.claim: Nafi, Hamza, Hafs, and Yaqub read إذ without alif and أدبر with it; the others read إذا and دبر, the latter matching the following oath wording.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p272/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p272/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p272/r1.claim: Both دبر and أدبر are Arabic forms for night’s departure; Abu Amr identifies دبر as Quraysh usage.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p272/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p272/r2.speaker: قطرب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p272/r2.claim: Qutrub says دبر can mean to arrive: Arabs say someone ‘came behind me,’ and night follows day.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r1.speaker: الشاعر
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r1.claim: A poet's verse and the idiom كأمس المدبر support the word's sense of what has passed.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r10.speaker: يونس بن حبيب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r10.claim: Yunus ibn Habib distinguishes دبر as passing away from أدبر as turning away.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r11.speaker: مجاهد وابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r11.claim: When Mujahid asked Ibn Abbas when night's dابر is, Ibn Abbas waited for the first caller to dawn prayer, then identified that time.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r12.speaker: قتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r12.claim: Qatada says دبر الليل means the night has departed.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r13.speaker: الأصمعي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r13.claim: Al-Asmaʿi's poem uses أمس الدابر as evidence for the phrase meaning the past or departed night.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r6.claim: كلا rebukes disbelievers and rebels; the oaths by moon, night, and morning honor their signs and direct reflection toward God, who sustains all existence.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r7.speaker: ابن كثير وابن عامر وأبو عمرو والكسائي وأبو بكر عن عاصم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r7.claim: These readers, along with many early authorities, read إذ أدبر with fatḥa on dāl and bāʾ.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r8.speaker: نافع وحمزة وحفص عن عاصم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r8.claim: These readers read إذا أدبر with still dāl and the quadriliteral verb.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r9.speaker: أبي بن كعب وابن مسعود
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r9.claim: Their codices have إذ أدبر with an alif and the quadriliteral form, also read by Hasan and other authorities.

TABRISI:74:32-56/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:74:32-56/r1.speaker: نافع وحمزة ويعقوب وخلف
TABRISI:74:32-56/r1.claim: These readers use ‘when the night passes’ without the alif in idh and with the alif in adbara; the other readers use the opposite forms.

TABRISI:74:32-56/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:74:32-56/r5.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:74:32-56/r5.claim: Dabar and adbar both mean that night has gone away or turned aside.

TABRISI:74:36-37/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:74:36-37/r7.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:74:36-37/r7.claim: The oath by the night may mean when it goes away; alternatively, dabbara means the night comes after the day and adbara means it departs as morning follows.

TABRISI:74:36-37/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:74:36-37/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:74:36-37/r8.claim: On another view, dabbara and adbara are two dialect forms with the same meaning, to pass away.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r1.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وابن عامر والكسائي وأبو بكر عن عاصم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r1.claim: They read idhā adbara, with alif and fatḥa on the dhāl.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r2.speaker: نافع وحمزة وحفص والفضل عن عاصم ويعقوب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r2.claim: They read idh adbara, with a still dhāl, no alif, and a still dāl.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r3.speaker: الفراء والأخفش وثعلب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r3.claim: The two readings may be synonymous dialect forms, as dabbara and adbara are both used of night or summer passing.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r4.speaker: أبو عبيدة وابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p409#2/r4.claim: Alternatively, dabbara means to come behind, while adbara means to depart.

QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r10.speaker: أبو عبيد
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r10.claim: Abu Ubayd prefers idha adbára because it matches the following idha asfara; he says Quranic oaths are followed by idha rather than idh.

QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r4.claim: Nafi, Hamza, and Hafs read “when the night turned away” with idh; other readers use idha, and some read dabbara without the prefix, forms treated as synonyms by al-Farra and al-Akhfash.

QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r5.claim: Some linguists distinguish dabbara, when night has passed, from adbára, when it begins to withdraw.

QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r6.claim: When Mujahid asked about idha dabbara, Ibn Abbas waited until night had passed and then said it was that moment.

QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r7.speaker: محمد بن السميقع
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r7.claim: Ibn al-Sumayqa reads the phrase with two alifs; the same form appears in the codices attributed to Abd Allah and Ubayy.

QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r8.speaker: قطرب
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r8.claim: Qutrub says readers of dabbara mean that night approaches from behind; Abu Amr calls it a Qurayshi usage.

QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r9.claim: In another report Ibn Abbas says adbára is correct, since a camel’s back is described as dabbara.

BAYDAWI-FULL:74:32-38/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:74:32-38/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:74:32-38/r3.claim: The night’s إدبار can mean withdrawal or, like أقبل, approach; Nafiʿ, Hamza, Yaʿqūb, and Ḥafṣ read دبر as a past verb.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p297#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p297#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p297#2/r1.claim: The readings “adbara” (attributed to Nāfiʿ, Ḥafṣ, Ḥamza, Yaʿqūb, and Khalaf) and “dabara” both mean the night departed; the latter may mean it came after daytime.

QASHANI:74:36/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:74:36/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:74:36/r2.claim: The moon is the receptive, clear heart; night is ego-darkness leaving as spirit-light splits through, and dawn is that light fully illuminating the heart.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r1.claim: The night’s retreat means that it has turned away; dabr and adbar can both mean departure. God swears by these signs to honor them and draw attention to divine wonders and the order of existence.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r2.speaker: ابن عباس وابن الزبير ومجاهد وعطاء وابن يعمر وأبو جعفر وشيبة وأبو الزناد وقتادة وعمر بن العزيز والحسن وطلحة والنحويان والابنان وأبو بكر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r2.claim: This reading has idha, a future-time adverb, with dabr in the form dabr; the following reading of dawn is parallel.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r3.speaker: ابن جبير والسلمي وابن سيرين والأعرج وزيد بن علي وأبو شيخ وابن محيصن ونافع وحمزة وحفص
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r3.claim: This reading has idh, a past-time adverb, followed by the quadriliteral adbara.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r4.speaker: الحسن وأبو رزين وأبو رجاء وابن يعمر والسلمي وطلحة والأعمش ويونس بن عبيد ومطر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r4.claim: A further reading uses idha and the hamzated adbara; its parallel with idha asfara is reflected in the codices of ʿAbd Allah and Ubayy.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r5.speaker: يونس بن حبيب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r5.claim: Yunus distinguishes dabr as ‘ended’ from adbara as ‘turned away.’

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r6.speaker: قتادة والزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r6.claim: Qatada glosses the night’s dabr as its turning away; al-Zamakhshari treats dabr as adbara, parallel to qabila and aqbala.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r7.claim: Another explanation takes the night’s departure as the day following it.

SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r1.speaker: نافع، حمزة، حفص
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r1.claim: Nafi‘, Hamza, and Hafs read ‘idh’ as a past-time adverb and ‘adbara’ as the quadriliteral verb; the written consonantal form also permits the alternative reading.

SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r2.speaker: أبو عبيد
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r2.claim: Abu Ubayd prefers ‘idha dabara’ because the next oath phrase also has ‘idha’; he notes that Abd Allah’s reading writes two alifs to represent the form with hamza.

SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas also prefers ‘idha’; a report says he objected to ‘adbara’ by saying that only a camel’s back turns away.

SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r4.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r4.claim: Al-Farra’ and al-Zajjaj regard dabara and adbara as synonymous, like other paired verbs meaning that night or day passed or turned away.

SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r5.speaker: يونس
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r5.claim: Yunus distinguishes the verbs: dabara means to end, while adbara means to turn away.

SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says dabara means adbara, as qabala means aqbala; one explanation is that night follows day.

SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r7.claim: The author cites ‘ams al-dabir’ and a poetic line as evidence for dabara meaning past or gone; ‘adbara’ for a rider approaching or leaving is quadriliteral only.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p233/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p233/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p233/r2.claim: The oath by the moon, night, and dawn reinforces the warning: the moon guides night travelers, while receding darkness and dawn's light portray knowledge and guidance displacing ignorance and doubt.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p233/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p233/r3.speaker: قطرب
BIQAI-FULL:v8p233/r3.claim: Qutrub allows adbara to mean that dawn approached, citing the Arab phrase meaning that someone came behind me.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p130/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p130/r7.speaker: ابن عباس وابن الزبير ومجاهد وعطاء وابن يعمر
ALUSI-FULL:v29p130/r7.claim: They read إذا دبر with dāl open, as the triliteral equivalent of أدبر or as the night following the day; the past form conveys certainty or is made future by إذا.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p130/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p130/r8.speaker: أبو رزين وأبو رجاء والأعمش ومطر ويونس بن عبيد
ALUSI-FULL:v29p130/r8.claim: They read إذا أدبر with hamza, also found in the codices of Abdullah and Ubayy; the form better pairs with the next verse's أسفر.

TABATABAI:74:35-38/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:74:35-38/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:74:35-38/r4.claim: The oath pairs night retreat with its opposite, the morning's unveiling; idbar is the reverse of the night's arrival, and isfar is the clearing of dawn.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p32/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p32/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p32/r4.claim: Nature’s manifestations argue for the Hereafter and expose heedlessness; the Qur’an warns so people can prepare, while evaders are left with stubbornness as their excuse.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r1.claim: The moon's slow phases answer why Judgment is delayed: humanity likewise advances through stages, and the Day comes at God's appointed time, when the universe's purpose is fulfilled.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r2.claim: The emphatic negation precedes the oath because the audience's denial is so objectionable that the speaker states rejection before giving its proof.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r3.claim: Qur'anic oaths substantiate a following claim; here they answer disbelievers asking why the promised Judgment has not arrived yet.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r1.claim: The signs of God follow a prescribed plan; only He knows its benefits, and justice will appear at its appointed time despite demands for haste.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r2.claim: The full moon in 84:18-19 signifies that humanity will ascend gradually to God's presence for accountability after successive stages.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r3.claim: Night yielding to morning illustrates this world's darkness giving way to Judgment at its appointed time, as surely as daily dawn arrives.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r4.claim: The daily alternation of night and dawn rehearses Judgment; nature continually supplies evidence of that Day for sincere truth-seekers.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:74:32/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:74:32/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:74:32/r1.claim: The oaths by the moon, departing night, and dawning morning draw attention both to divine signs and to the importance of the warning to humanity.

QIRAAT-ER:74:33:3#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:74:33:3#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:74:33:3#1/r1.claim: The reading changes idh to idhā and adbara to dabara, broadening the temporal reference and verb form.

STUDYQURAN:74:32/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:74:32/r1.speaker: Āl, Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:74:32/r1.claim: “Nay” rejects claims that people can know God’s hosts’ number or overcome them; the oath also recalls other oaths on the moon and the night-day alternation.
